text: staging plays an important role in determining treatment. The management of SCLC differs significantly from that of non-small cell types. The mainstay of treatment for small cell lung cancer is chemotherapy.1-5 In limited disease (disease limited to one hemithorax with hilar and mediastinal lymph node in- volvement that can be encompassed within one tolerable radiotherapy field) the combination of chemotherapy and chest radiotherapy has been shown to improve survival6,7 and is recommended therapy.2-5 The most common chem- otherapy regimen is 4 to 6 cycles of etoposide and cisplatin (EP or PE),1,3-5,7,8 which offers a survival advantage over the previously used regimen of cyclophosphamide, doxo- rubicin, and vincristine (CAV). The optimum scheduling of chemotherapy and radiotherapy has been investigated and concurrent therapy found to be superior to sequential radiotherapy.3,5 In comparing early and late concurrent therapy, a meta-analysis9 of 7 studies found that a small improvement in overall survival at 2 years was associated with early radiotherapy (begun within 9 weeks of starting chemotherapy, or before the third cycle of chemotherapy) compared with late radiotherapy. There was also evidence that the use of hyperfractionated radiotherapy (given twice daily) and platinum-based regimens contributed to this benefit. In general, for limited disease it is recommended2,3,5,7 that concurrent chest radiotherapy should be started with the first or second chemotherapy cy- cle. Response rates of 70 to 90% are reported, but median survival rates are only 14 to 20 months and the 2-year sur- vival rate is about 40%.5 Only a few patients present with resectable early stage dis- ease. Careful pre-operative staging is essential to rule out nodal involvement, and all patients should receive adju- vant chemotherapy. If nodal metastases are found, the ad- dition of postoperative chest radiotherapy should be con- sidered. Patients with later disease stages do not benefit from surgery.3,5 In extensive SCLC (spread beyond one hemithorax and may include malignant pleural or pericardial effusion or haematogenous spread) chemotherapy alone is used to palliate symptoms and prolong survival. The combination of etoposide and cisplatin (or carboplatin) is also used in these patients3,5,7 but response is poorer than that for limit- ed disease, with response rates of 60 to 70% and a 2-year survival rate of less than 5%.5 The use of consolidation or maintenance chemotherapy has been studied in both limit- ed and extensive disease. Most studies have found no im- provement in progression-free or overall survival, and the general recommendation is that such extra therapy, with its associated toxicity, should not be used.1-5,8 This view has been challenged by a meta-analysis10 of 14 studies sug- gesting that there is evidence for benefit from maintenance therapy, although it is unclear which patients might benefit and which regimen would be most effective.
